title: 5. Leading Operational KPIs, Structural Potential & CEO Walk-the-Talk

epigraph.quote: Underwriting Rule: trust a management's description of the future in proportion to the accuracy of its description of the past.
epigraph.author: Research Desk house maxim

web_blocks.html: Reported profit tells you what the business earned. It does not tell you what it is about to earn. For MPS the quantities that move first are not exotic. They are how much of each rupee of revenue survives as segment margin and how many people it takes to produce that rupee. They are how concentrated the customer list is, how much of the book renews without being re-won, and how quickly invoices turn into cash. I tested a longer list against the evidence and kept six. For each I give the baseline (FY22 or FY24 where a comparable exists), the audited FY26 figure and the latest reading (Q1 and Q2 FY27, results of 3-4 November 2026). I also give a forward threshold and the source. Note one trap. In Q1 FY26 management restated all periods into Research, Education and Corporate Learning [10]. Segment baselines before FY25 are therefore on the old Content, Platform and eLearning basis, and are flagged as not like-for-like.

web_blocks.caption: Six leading KPIs for MPS: baseline, FY26, latest and forward watch threshold
web_blocks.takeaway: Read down the 'latest' column and you see a business running at record margins on flat headcount, with concentration falling and cash converting. Read down the 'watch' column and you see where it can crack. Research margin is the profit pool, about 65% of FY26 segment EBITDA (computed from the segment note). A pass-through of AI savings to clients is therefore the single most consequential risk. Numbers marked 'derived' were computed by Python from the AR26 segment note (segment result plus depreciation).

web_blocks.html: Two data points in that table deserve a flag. Management's own numbers on Unbound's entry margin disagree. The CEO said on the Q2 FY27 call that 'we started off at what, 12%, 13% when we bought the company' [2]. The CFO said the first 49 to 50 days came in at 18.5 to 19% [19]. The concentration series also changes its basis. The Q2 FY25 call quoted a top-10 share of 48% [8]. The Q1 FY26 earnings deck shows top-10 at 44% for Q1 FY25 and 59% for Q1 FY26 [24]. I trust the direction of the largest-customer number, from 11.9% in FY23 to 17.3% in FY26. It comes from the audited segment note [15, 1]. In FY27 the AJE revenue contraction and Unbound's many small accounts then pull the top-5 share back down.

web_blocks.caption: Quarterly sales growth and operating margin from the blind snapshot (the quarterly shape of the AJE inflation and pruning)
web_blocks.takeaway: In the snapshot, quarterly operating margin rose from 23% in June 2024 (the quarter AJE arrived loss-making) to 34% in both June and September 2026. Year-on-year sales growth peaked at +39% in December 2024. It turned to -2% in December 2025 as AJE was pruned. It recovered to +20% and +15% in the two latest quarters. That is the leading-indicator story in one table. Margin repaired first, and growth followed two to three quarters later.

web_blocks.html: Now capacity and structural potential. MPS's annual report cites a global addressable market of more than US$800 billion. It builds that from several pieces. Education solutions are about US$416 billion in 2025, heading for about US$878 billion by 2031. Corporate e-learning is about US$353 billion in 2025, heading for about US$874 billion by 2030. Research output was about 3.5 million science and engineering articles in 2024. A new healthcare-knowledge adjacency completes the list [1]. Those are company-cited figures, and I could not independently verify the two large market sizes. Aggregator listings I came across put STM publishing anywhere between about US$13 billion and about US$41 billion (search snippets; I did not read those reports). That tells you how soft such numbers are. The better evidence is volume. The STM Association reports that gold open access reached 44% of all global articles in 2025, with nearly two million articles. That implies roughly 4.5 million articles a year (my arithmetic). It also reports fast growth in research output from China and India [73]. Nature counted more than 10,000 retractions in 2023 as publishers struggled with sham papers and peer-review fraud [74]. The company's own report cites 14,000 retraction notices, a different count [1]. Either way, integrity screening is a real and growing workload.

The sharper way to size the opportunity is management's own. On the Q4 FY26 call an analyst quoted a slide saying MPS has only a 0.5% share of its total serviceable market. The CEO answered that the question is how to go from 0.5% to 1% and then 2% [19]. FY26 revenue of Rs 768 Cr at 0.5% implies a serviceable market of about Rs 1.54 lakh Cr. At the Rs 85.09 per dollar implied in Unbound's price, that is roughly US$18 billion. This is my arithmetic from Rs 140.40 Cr and US$16.5 million [1, 18]. The figure is about 2% of the US$800 billion headline. One percent of it is about Rs 1,536 Cr, which is almost exactly the Vision 2027 revenue target. The runway is real, but the quoted total market is not the relevant denominator.

web_blocks.caption: Structural potential by segment: sourced market context, binding constraint, and what would relax it
web_blocks.takeaway: The binding constraint differs by segment. Research is limited by price pass-through and customer concentration rather than by demand. Education is limited by US adoption calendars and public funding. Corporate Learning is limited by the quality of the book it kept after running off compliance work. In none of the three is the constraint 'not enough market'.

web_blocks.html: What caps the ceiling, then, is not a shortage of demand. It is three other things. The first is people. MPS has more than 3,200 colleagues and a Tier-2 India delivery base. It also runs a deliberate core-plus-flex model that lets cost scale with revenue [1, 19]. The second is client budgets. One customer is 17.3% of revenue. The CEO himself pointed to US federal research and nursing budgets as swing factors [1, 2]. The third is unit price. The CEO's framing on the Q4 FY26 call was that “AI is going to super-compress the price of commoditized production work” [19]. He added that this work would concentrate in a few scaled suppliers. The arithmetic of deflation is brutal and worth keeping in your head. A 20% price cut needs 25% more volume to hold revenue, because 1 divided by 0.8 is 1.25. A 20% cut is the size of the FY20 offshore book-production cut [12]. On the Q2 FY27 call the CEO said “Customers expect to share in our productivity, and they do, but we kind of make that up through more volume” [2]. That claim is the one the Research margin KPI above is built to test.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S NOTE: Paid for outcomes, or paid for hours?
paragraphs: Management's strategic claim since Q1 FY27 is that revenue is shifting from effort to outcome. It says 25% of revenue is outcome-based and 45% recurring [25]. If that is true, AI helps MPS. The price attaches to the result, such as a manuscript accepted, a paper mill caught or a subscription renewed. Productivity gains then stay with the vendor. If it is mostly rhetoric, AI is the same price-cut cycle as FY20, only faster.

Our independent judgment: the margin evidence is real. Research margin went from 36.8% in FY25 to 48.2% in Q2 FY27 on near-flat headcount. But no audited disclosure defines 'outcome-based' or 'AI-attached' revenue, and the annual report gives no figure. The KPI to watch is therefore not the headline percentage. It is whether the margin survives the first contract renewal where a large customer asks for its share of the productivity.

web_blocks.html: Now the audit that matters most for how much weight to put on forecasts. What did management say, in its own words, and what did the accounts later show? I took twelve specific, dated promises from the earnings calls and annual reports. The Q4 FY26 call transcript is not in the standard library. I took it from the company's own exchange filing of 25 May 2026 [19]. A scorecard comes first, then discussion.

web_blocks.caption: CEO and CFO walk-the-talk scorecard: twelve dated promises against reported outcomes
web_blocks.takeaway: Tally: two DELIVERED, three DELIVERED WITH COST, three PARTIAL, two MISSED and two TOO EARLY. The pattern is consistent. On numbers management can see (EPS, group margin, EBITDA floor) it has delivered or beaten what it said. On turnarounds and deal timing, which depend on third parties and customers, it has run late or short. Corporate Learning missed three separate timelines. The acquisition cadence has been slower than the pipeline language implied.

web_blocks.html: Where did management over-promise? In three places, and they share a cause. First, Corporate Learning. Management gave three different dates for the turn: margins 'here to stay' in February 2025, a 'banner year' for FY26, and take-off 'from Q2' in May 2025. The segment then shrank 16.5% with EBITDA down about a third [22, 20, 19]. Second, acquisition cadence. 'One or two a year' and 'five deals lined up back-to-back' produced one deal in twelve months [17]. Third, AJE growth. The thesis in November 2024 was strong organic growth. The reality was a planned shrink of more than a quarter [8, 1]. The shared cause is that all three depend on external timing (customers, sellers, regulators) and on a leader who is optimistic about timelines. Where management controls the variable, it has under-promised. EPS above Rs 100 was guided when 75% of the year was reported. The FY27 EBITDA figure has already been raised. The margin guide was exceeded.

The governance lens adds two cautions from the audited accounts. FY26's net exceptional item was a Rs 7.64 Cr gain. It nets Rs 29.68 Cr of write-backs against Rs 22.03 Cr of charges. The write-backs include Rs 13.95 Cr of AJE customer advances and Rs 15.73 Cr of Liberate liabilities. The charges are Rs 12.93 Cr of Liberate goodwill impairment, Rs 7.01 Cr of labour-code impact and Rs 2.09 Cr of AJE restructuring [1]. The Chairman's letter says charges were taken 'cleanly through the profit and loss account' [1]. That is true of the charges, but the write-backs offset them in the same line. Goodwill of Rs 376.32 Cr is 40% of total assets. The integration record in rows 5 and 7 therefore matters more than the headline growth rate [1].

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S NOTE: Floors, not ceilings
paragraphs: The CEO asked listeners to read the FY27 guidance “as a floor, not as a target we hope to reach” [25]. The Q4 FY26 call defended it as 'built bottom-up' and organic [19]. That framing is credible. The same management exceeded its FY26 EPS promise and raised the FY27 floor within six months.

Our judgment: treat management's numeric guidance as reliable and its qualitative timelines as optimistic. The one number that is a stretch rather than a floor is the FY28 Rs 1,500 Cr revenue target. By management's own admission it depends on acquisitions that have not yet been announced.

web_blocks.html: What would change our view of the business (quality triggers only): (1) Research EBITDA margin below 40% for two consecutive quarters while revenue still grows. That would mean AI savings are being passed through faster than volume recovers them. (2) The top-5 share back above 50%, or the largest customer reaching 20% of revenue. (3) Unbound's first full-cycle institutional renewal below 90%, against the 97% Unbound claims. (4) Corporate Learning margin back under 20%, or revenue falling again for two quarters. (5) Headcount growing faster than revenue for two quarters, which would end the operating-leverage story.

book_paragraphs: Let me ask you something before we dig into the numbers. When a company hands you its quarterly results, do you read them as a verdict or as a forecast? Most people read them as a verdict. But profit is a lagging thing: it is the harvest of decisions made six to eighteen months earlier. If you want to know what the harvest will look like next year, you have to look at the seedbed. For MPS, I think the seedbed has six measurements, and I want to walk you through them the way I would walk through a plant with a production manager who knows where the bodies are buried.

Start with Research margin, because that is where most of the money is. Picture one of the five largest companies in MPS's market, which the research team said is moving more than 110,000 submissions a year onto MPS's peer-review platform. Every manuscript passes through checks for fabricated data, image manipulation, language and format, and then through reviewers. MPS runs that desk. Its tools now do a lot of the checking, and the Research segment's margin climbed from about 37% in FY25 to 48% in the September 2026 quarter. Here is the question that decides everything: when the publisher notices that the checking is less costly to do, how much of the saving does it ask for back? The CEO's answer on the Q2 FY27 call was “Customers expect to share in our productivity, and they do, but we kind of make that up through more volume.” I would not take that on faith; I would watch whether the margin holds through the next renewal.

The second measurement is the one I like best because it is hard to fake: revenue growth, profit growth and headcount growth side by side. In the first quarter of FY27 revenue grew 20%, EBITDA grew 53% and headcount grew less than 3%. That is operating leverage, the very thing every services company promises and almost none delivers. The warning sign would be the reverse: headcount growing faster than revenue. Management admits it hired ahead of new mandates in the second quarter, so this is a number to watch each quarter, not once a year.

Third, who pays you? In FY26 one customer accounted for Rs 133 crore of revenue, 17.3% of the group, up from 11.9% three years earlier. The top five clients were about 45% of revenue in early FY26 and 46% in the latest quarter, down from 51% a year before. That decline is partly arithmetic: Unbound Medicine brought hundreds of small institutional accounts, so the client count jumped from 422 to 839. The CEO's argument is that this lowers concentration and adds predictability, and he is right on the arithmetic. What the table cannot tell you is how the large relationships are going, which is why I put the threshold on the largest customer, not the average.

Fourth, how much of the book repeats without being re-won? The CEO said in August 2026 that 45% of revenue is recurring and 25% is outcome-based. Unbound itself claims a 97% annual renewal rate among its institutional customers. The CEO's rule is “It should show up in our revenue, not on slides,” and those are promising words, but notice that neither figure appears in the audited accounts, so I treat them as claims to be checked against the first full renewal cycle, which the CEO himself says the company is still learning.

Fifth, the turnaround margins. Corporate Learning was the segment that went wrong in FY26: revenue fell 16.5%, EBITDA about a third, and by the Q3 call the three operating businesses were all below the prior year and budget. The fix was radical, with about a third fewer people and the old compliance work deliberately run off, and the margin recovered to about 25% by Q1 FY27. Unbound's margin is the other turnaround: management says it was between 12 and 19% depending on who you ask and the date, and the plan is to exit FY27 at 25 to 30%.

Sixth, cash. Collections are the plainest test of whether customers value what they are billed for. Days sales outstanding fell from 53 in March 2025 to 38 in September 2026, and operating cash flow was 83% of EBITDA in FY26 after a weak 48% in FY25, against a ten-year average of about 72%. The company repaid the loan it took for Unbound within six months and now has about Rs 163 crore in cash and no debt.

And the runway? Management's own sizing is the most useful: it says it has about 0.5% of its serviceable market. At FY26 revenue, that implies a serviceable market of about US$18 billion, not the US$800 billion in the glossy deck, and getting to 1% would roughly equal the Vision 2027 revenue target. The ceiling is therefore not demand. It is people, client budgets, and the price of the work as AI makes it less costly to produce.

book_callouts.title: Narrator's reflection: floors, ceilings and timelines
book_callouts.quote: Trust a management's description of the future in proportion to the accuracy of its description of the past.
book_callouts.text: When I audited twelve dated promises, a pattern leapt out. Where management controls the variable (an EPS threshold, a margin range, an EBITDA floor) it has been conservative and has delivered or beaten. Where success depends on customers, sellers or timing (a turnaround in Corporate Learning, the pace of acquisitions, growth in an acquired business) it has been optimistic and has run late. A sensible reader treats the first kind of promise as a floor and the second as a hope.
bullets: Two promises delivered, three delivered at a cost, three partial, two missed and two too early to call.
The FY28 Rs 1,500 crore revenue target needs about 40% annual growth from FY26 and, by management's own words, acquisitions that have not yet been announced.
The cleanest evidence of AI productivity is margin on flat headcount, not a disclosed AI revenue line.

book_subsections.title: The audit, promise by promise
paragraphs: Let me take you through a few of the promises, because the pattern shows up better in the specifics. In November 2024 the CEO told analysts he felt very comfortable sustaining a margin of 30 to 32%. FY25 came in at 29%, a shade under, but FY26 was 30.7% and the first half of FY27 was 34.3%. Delivered, and then some. In the same call he said FY26 would be a big, big banner year for the e-learning business, and three months later the segment head said its margins were here to stay. Then reality: Corporate Learning revenue fell 16.5% and EBITDA fell about a third. That promise was missed, and missed three different ways.

Now the one I find most instructive, AJE. The CEO called it MPS 2.0 when it was acquired: another business with an obvious fix. And the fix worked. AJE's margin went from the low twenties to above 30% within a year, and its American entity earned Rs 52 crore before tax in FY26 against a purchase price of Rs 70 crore. But the promised strong organic growth did not arrive: AJE's revenue fell by almost a third as management pruned what it called an inflated base. A margin promise kept, a growth promise reversed. It is why I call it delivered with a cost.

And then there is the promise that quietly changed. In late 2024 and early 2025 the CEO said the company would stop giving short-term guidance because it was a distraction. By May 2026 it had guided EBITDA for FY27 above Rs 300 crore, and by November it had raised the floor to Rs 310 crore. I do not mark them down for that; more disclosure is better. But it does tell you that stated policies on communication are not binding, and that is useful to know.

Two more promises round out the picture. The first is about capital. For years the company has said it funds deals from cash first, debt second and equity last, and that capital must earn its return within twelve months or go back to shareholders. In FY26 it paid for most of Unbound from cash, borrowed Rs 42 crore for four years, repaid the loan in six months, and skipped the final dividend. You can call that discipline or you can call it flexibility; both words fit. The second is the Vision 2027 target of Rs 1,500 crore of revenue by FY28. The halfway mark was reached on schedule in FY25, though roughly nine-tenths of that year's increase came from AJE. The rest of the climb, at about 40% a year from FY26, would need acquisitions the company has not yet announced; at the pace of the latest half-year, organic growth alone gets to roughly Rs 1,070 crore. The CEO calls the target intact and in absolute line of sight. I would call it a stretch whose outcome depends on a deal pipeline more than on the operating engine.

book_subsections.title: Where the optimism lives
paragraphs: If I had to summarise management's forecasting style in one sentence, it would be: precise where it controls the lever, hopeful where someone else does. Consider the acquisition pipeline. In May 2025 the CEO said the company usually does one or two acquisitions a year. In November 2025 he said five deals were lined up back to back and that Rs 300 to 400 crore of acquisitions could be completed in twelve to eighteen months. A year later, one deal has closed, for Rs 140 crore, and the CEO says he would rather miss a deal than overpay. That is disciplined, but it is not the pace described.

There is a related point about the equity raising. In May 2025 the company had obtained an enabling resolution for a possible fund-raise to support a very large acquisition of Rs 300 to 700 crore. By November the thinking had become that debt should come first, with up to Rs 200 crore of borrowing, and equity was not on the cards for the near future. A prudent change of mind, but note the reversal.

The CEO's own explanation is that the company has always been conservative on numbers and that the few times it guided it comfortably beat the guidance. For the FY26 EPS promise, that is true, though the bar was low: nine months of earnings per share were already Rs 74.39, so only Rs 25.61 was needed in the final quarter, when the previous year's fourth quarter had delivered Rs 27.52.

book_subsections.title: The AI pricing question, honestly
paragraphs: The question every reader of this chapter should be asking is whether AI helps this company or hollows it out. Think about what happened in FY20: customers cut offshore production prices by about 20% on average, journals volume went to lower-priced vendors, and revenue and profit fell together. That was a human-labour price war. AI could be a much faster version of it. A competitor, Straive, markets to publishers on the promise of 30 to 40% lower operating costs, and says so on its website. That is the pressure MPS must absorb.

The CEO's argument is a bifurcation: AI compresses the price of commoditised work such as basic copy-editing and page-based content, while demand for trusted AI inside high-stakes workflows (peer review integrity, clinical answers, accessibility) expands. Notice the logic: commoditised work goes to a few scaled suppliers, which is where a company with 200 AI engineers wants to be. A twenty percent price cut needs twenty-five percent more volume to hold revenue; MPS has shown revenue growing 17 to 20% in the latest two quarters with headcount nearly flat. So far the evidence leans his way. In the CEO's words, “The risk for us is not that AI will displace us.” The risk, he says, is standing still while the market splits. The proof will be in the margin at the next big renewal.
